docs.title: Project CodeGuard: Security Skills and Rules for AI Coding Agents
docs.text: Project CodeGuard is an open-source, model-agnostic security framework that embeds secure-by-default practices into AI coding agent workflows. It provides security guidance that AI assistants can use during code generation and review.

docs.title: Why Project CodeGuard?
docs.text:
AI coding agents can produce code that omits important security controls or uses unsafe patterns. Common problems include:

  • Missing input validation
  • Hardcoded secrets and credentials
  • Weak cryptographic algorithms
  • Unsafe functions
  • Missing authentication or authorization checks

CodeGuard makes relevant security guidance available while an agent plans, implements, or reviews a change. For example, its input-validation guidance can help an agent choose appropriate checks during implementation and identify missing checks during review.

The results still need independent testing and review because they depend on the client, model, and task.

docs.title: Security Coverage
docs.text:
Our rules cover essential security domains:

  • Cryptography: Safe algorithms (including post-quantum cryptography), secure key management, certificate validation
  • Input Validation: SQL injection prevention, XSS protection, command injection defense
  • Authentication: MFA best practices, OAuth/OIDC, secure session management
  • Authorization: RBAC/ABAC, access control, IDOR prevention
  • Supply Chain: Dependency security, SBOM generation, vulnerability management
  • Cloud Security: IaC hardening, container security, Kubernetes best practices
  • Platform Security: Mobile apps, web services, API security
  • Data Protection: Privacy, encryption at rest/transit, secure storage

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
CodeGuard is an Agent Skill: a folder of instructions and security guidance for your coding agent. For personal use, install a released version in your user skill directory so it is available across projects.

  1. Download Source code (zip) from the latest release and extract it. The skill folder is skills/codeguard/ inside the extracted directory.
  2. Copy that complete codeguard/ folder to your client's personal skill location:
Client Personal skill location Claude Code ~/.claude/skills/codeguard/ Codex ~/.agents/skills/codeguard/

Here, ~ means your home directory. For other clients, use their supported Agent Skills location. 3. Start a new client session and ask: “Use CodeGuard to review this authentication code for security issues.”

See Getting Started for updating an existing installation, project-level installation, and plugin options.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
CodeGuard gives your agent security guidance to consult while planning, writing, or reviewing code. The skill's instructions describe when to use that guidance and how to apply it to the task.

Use CodeGuard alongside your existing tests, security scanners, and human review. For more focused tasks, the repository also includes security-review and memory-safe-migration workflows.

docs.title: CodeGuard Claude Code Plugin
docs.text: The Claude Code plugin includes CodeGuard and the security-review and memory-safe-migration skills.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
With Claude Code installed, run these commands in your terminal:

claude plugin marketplace add cosai-oasis/project-codeguard
claude plugin install codeguard-security@project-codeguard

Start a new Claude Code session and use the skill with your task:

/codeguard-security:codeguard Review this authentication code for security issues.

The plugin manifest registers skills/ and sources/skills/.

docs.title: CodeGuard Codex Plugin
docs.text: The Codex plugin includes the primary CodeGuard skill.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
With Codex CLI installed, run these commands in your terminal:

codex plugin marketplace add cosai-oasis/project-codeguard
codex plugin add codeguard-security@project-codeguard

Start a new Codex session and select CodeGuard from the skill picker, or include it in your request:

$codeguard Review this authentication code for security issues.

The plugin manifest registers skills/. The additional skills are available separately in the repository.

docs.title: Custom Rules
docs.text:
Instructions for contributing changes to CodeGuard's guidance are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

Instructions for the retired native-rule converter are preserved in the v1.5.0 documentation.

docs.title: Q: Where can I access the rules?
docs.text: A: You can access the rules in the Project CodeGuard GitHub repository. The latest stable release is available on the releases page.

docs.title: Q: How do I install the rules?
docs.text: A: See Getting Started for plugin and skill-folder installation instructions.

docs.title: Q: Will these rules consume a lot of the AI agent's context window?
docs.text: A: Context use depends on the client, task, and amount of guidance loaded. CodeGuard does not have a fixed context cost; refer to the skill definition for its current instructions and supporting material.

docs.title: Q: What is the difference between always-on rules and glob-scoped rules?
docs.text: A: These terms describe activation in the legacy native rule bundles. The current distribution provides an Agent Skill; its intended use is described in the skill definition.

docs.title: Q: What are the OWASP supplementary rules?
docs.text: A: The sources/rules/owasp/ collection contains OWASP-based guidance used by the security-review workflow. It is separate from the primary CodeGuard skill and is not included in its release archive.

docs.title: Q: Why does the downloaded release folder appear empty?
docs.text: A: Legacy native bundles use hidden dot-directories; follow the v1.5.0 installation guide. The skill archive uses a visible codeguard/ directory.

docs.title: Q: Can I use this with Claude Code?
docs.text: A: Yes. Follow the Claude Code plugin instructions.

docs.title: Q: How can I report a problem or enhancement to any of the rules?
docs.text: A: Open an issue with the affected guidance, client and model, and a reproducible example.

docs.title: Q: How can I contribute to these rules and this project?
docs.text: A: Follow CONTRIBUTING.md for proposing changes, validation, and pull requests.

docs.title: Q: Does Project CodeGuard replace my security scanners?
docs.text: A: No. CodeGuard provides guidance to the agent; it does not guarantee review coverage or detection of vulnerabilities. Use it alongside your existing security scanners, functional tests, and human review.

docs.title: Still have questions?
docs.text: If your question is not covered here, open an issue or start a discussion with the community.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: The CodeGuard skill is maintained in skills/codeguard/. This folder contains the skill definition and its supporting guidance. Use the complete folder when installing CodeGuard; no conversion step is required.

docs.title: Project CodeGuard Introduction Video
docs.text: This video introduces Project CodeGuard and includes several demos on how to use it during code generation and code review with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.

docs.title: Choose an install path
docs.text: For individual use, install a released version in your personal skill directory. This makes CodeGuard available across your projects. A project-level installation is useful when a team wants to track the skill with a particular repository.

docs.title: Install for yourself
docs.text:
1. Open the latest release, download Source code (zip), and extract it.
  2. Locate skills/codeguard/ inside the extracted directory and copy the complete folder to your client's personal skill location:
Client Personal skill location Claude Code ~/.claude/skills/codeguard/ Codex ~/.agents/skills/codeguard/
  1. Start a new client session and ask the agent to use CodeGuard for a coding or review task.

These paths apply to local client sessions; ~ means your home directory. For other clients, use their supported Agent Skills location.

If CodeGuard is already installed, preserve the previous copy and replace the complete folder rather than merging versions.

docs.title: Install for a project
docs.text:
Use the same released skills/codeguard/ folder, but copy it into the target repository:

Client Project skill location Claude Code .claude/skills/codeguard/ Codex .agents/skills/codeguard/

These paths are relative to the target repository's root. Include the installed files in version control so the team can review updates with the project.

docs.title: Plugin installation
docs.text: The Claude Code plugin and Codex plugin provide another installation option. Use one installation route per client to avoid competing copies of CodeGuard.

docs.title: Skill release archive
docs.text:
The release workflow packages the primary skill as codeguard-skill.zip and publishes its checksum in SHA256SUMS. For a release that includes these assets, download both files from that release into a new directory. The following command verifies the checksum before extracting the archive.

shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS && unzip codeguard-skill.zip

The archive contains codeguard/ and LICENSE.md. Install the complete codeguard/ folder at your chosen skill location.

docs.title: CodeGuard guidance
docs.text: The skill definition describes CodeGuard's instructions and supporting guidance. CodeGuard is advisory; its availability or use does not establish that generated code is correct or secure.

docs.title: Additional workflows
docs.text: The repository also contains the security-review and memory-safe-migration workflows in sources/skills/. The Claude Code plugin registers both workflows, and their source folders are available for other integrations.

docs.title: Previous native integrations
docs.text: Native rule bundles and the MCP server remain available in the v1.5.0 release and source. Follow the tagged installation guide for those assets. Existing security-review users should update their installed copy so its core-guidance links point to skills/codeguard/rules/.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text: Start with the FAQ for common questions. You can also report a bug or ask a question, or join the community discussion.

docs.title: CodeGuard MCP Server
docs.text:
The MCP server implementation is no longer included on main. Its v1.5.0 documentation and source remain available for existing deployments.

For the current skill installation, see Getting Started.

docs.title: CoSAI Personas for Project CodeGuard
docs.text:
Project CodeGuard aligns with the CoSAI standard personas so that deployment responsibilities are described using the same vocabulary used across the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI) ecosystem.

This page summarizes each persona in the context of deploying and operating CodeGuard so that install-path and test-plan documentation can reference a shared mental model.

Scope of this page

This page does not replace the upstream CoSAI persona definitions. It explains how each persona typically shows up when implementing CodeGuard across individual developers, teams, and organizations.

docs.title: Persona Summary
docs.text: Persona Role in CodeGuard deployment Application Developer Installs CodeGuard into repositories and user profiles; consumes rules through their AI coding tool. AI System Governance Defines and enforces org-wide CodeGuard policy; owns vendor dashboards and managed-settings deployments. Agentic Platform and Framework Providers Provide the IDEs, agent frameworks, and plugin marketplaces that discover and invoke CodeGuard skills. AI Platform Provider Operates internal skill distribution and device-management-managed client configuration. AI System Users Developers and other end users who benefit from CodeGuard-guided AI output but do not configure the install path. Model Provider Upstream model developer; not a CodeGuard implementer but benefits from CodeGuard nudging safe patterns at the tool layer. Data Provider Supplies data used to train or evaluate models; out of scope for install path implementation. AI Model Serving Operates runtime model-serving infrastructure; out of scope for CodeGuard install path implementation.

docs.title: Personas Directly Involved in CodeGuard Install Paths
Application Developer
docs.text:
The most common persona implementing CodeGuard.

  • Installs CodeGuard skills into repositories and user profiles.
  • Updates installed skills or plugins from an approved CodeGuard revision or release.
  • Uses the AI tool (Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, etc.) that consumes CodeGuard.
  • Can operate either at user scope (personal machine) or project scope (committed to a repo).

Typical install routes owned

  • Agent Skills (project and user scope)
  • Plugin marketplace (Claude Code, Codex)
  • Direct skill installation from source

docs.title: AI System Governance
docs.text:
Represents AI risk, security, and compliance owners at the organization level.

  • Decides which CodeGuard rules are mandatory for the organization.
  • Owns organizational settings and policies for approved CodeGuard installations.
  • Reviews and approves rule updates landing in repositories through PRs.
  • Defines audit, rollback, and change-control procedures for CodeGuard rollouts.

Typical install routes owned

  • Org-managed vendor dashboards
  • Policy review for project-scoped installations

docs.title: Agentic Platform and Framework Providers
docs.text:
Providers of the IDEs, agent frameworks, and orchestration tools that actually consume CodeGuard rules.

  • Define how skills are discovered and invoked.
  • Determine how managed settings and marketplaces are enforced.
  • Shape the effective guarantees CodeGuard can make in each tool.

Examples

  • IDEs and coding agents: Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity, OpenClaw, Hermes
  • Agent frameworks and orchestration: LangChain, Semantic Kernel, and similar

Typical install routes influenced

  • Agent Skills activation behavior
  • Plugin marketplace enforcement
  • Managed settings propagation
  • Org-wide skill distribution

docs.title: AI Platform Provider
docs.text:
Platform, SRE, or infrastructure teams that host shared services supporting CodeGuard at scale.

  • Manages device management (MDM/Jamf/Intune) flows that push managed settings.
  • Runs the CI/CD and artifact pipelines used to build and distribute CodeGuard packages inside an organization.
  • Handles uptime, observability, rollback, and access control for shared CodeGuard infrastructure.

Typical install routes owned

  • Internal redistribution of approved CodeGuard skills and release artifacts
  • Endpoint-managed settings deployment

docs.title: AI System Users
docs.text:
End users consuming AI-assisted output produced by tools that have CodeGuard applied.

  • Typically do not configure CodeGuard themselves.
  • Benefit from secure-by-default behavior shaped by CodeGuard rules.
  • May request new rules or report false positives, feeding back into other personas.

docs.title: Model Provider
docs.text:
• Provides the underlying models used by coding agents.
  • Does not implement CodeGuard install paths, but benefits when CodeGuard shapes prompts and outputs toward safer patterns.

docs.title: Data Provider
docs.text:
• Supplies training, evaluation, or inference data to model providers.
  • Not directly involved in CodeGuard install path implementation.

docs.title: AI Model Serving
docs.text:
• Operates runtime environments that serve model predictions.
  • Not directly involved in CodeGuard install path implementation, though CodeGuard-guided client-side behavior can reduce unsafe patterns reaching the serving layer.

docs.title: Persona-to-Install-Route Mapping
docs.text: For current plugin and skill-folder installation routes, see Getting Started. Application Developers typically own individual and repository installations, AI System Governance reviews organizational adoption, and AI Platform Providers operate internal distribution.

docs.title: Authored Skills
docs.text:
The primary CodeGuard skill guides coding and review. The repository also includes the workflows described below in sources/skills/ for more focused tasks.

Skill Purpose security-review Review a repository and produce a structured Markdown report. memory-safe-migration Plan and carry out migration of memory-unsafe code, including FFI boundaries.

Both are registered by the Claude Code plugin and are available as source folders for other integrations. The Codex plugin registers only CodeGuard. See Getting Started for installation instructions.

docs.title: Security Review
docs.text:
The security-review skill defines a repository review that produces findings, remediation guidance, and a record of coverage. Its input is the target repository.

The workflow asks the agent to save a Markdown report at ./security_report/sec_review_<repo-name>_<YYYY-MM-DD_HH-mm-ss>.md. This path is relative to the agent's working directory. Review the findings and claimed coverage before relying on the report.

The skill definition defines the task inputs and report requirements. Its review guidelines describe rule loading and the detailed procedure.

docs.title: Memory-Safe Migration
docs.text:
The memory-safe-migration skill helps assess C/C++ migration, select a memory-safe language, and review boundaries between safe and unsafe code.

The skill definition owns the migration sequence and priorities. Its assessment script and references support planning, FFI design, and validation. Keep these files with the skill when installing it.

docs.title: Project Decisions
docs.text: Project decision records preserve choices that shape CodeGuard's scope, architecture, or contributor expectations. They capture why a decision was made so contributors do not need to reconstruct it from meetings or issue history.

docs.title: Decision Registry
docs.text: Record Status Date 0001: Separate Guidance from Runtime and Scanning Accepted 2026-07-14

docs.title: When to Write a Decision Record
docs.text:
Create a record when a decision:

  • establishes a project boundary or long-lived technical direction;
  • affects multiple features or contributors; or
  • is likely to be revisited without durable context.

Use issues and pull requests for routine implementation choices. Decision records should add context, not duplicate those discussions.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Copy the template to the next available four-digit number.
  2. Name the file NNNN-short-title.md using lowercase, hyphen-separated words.
  3. Set the status to Proposed, identify an owner, add the record to this registry, and open a pull request with the relevant issue links.
  4. Review the proposal through the repository's contribution process. Before merging an approved proposal, change its status to Accepted and update its date. Close rejected proposals with the rationale recorded in the pull request.
  5. Do not rewrite an accepted decision when the direction changes. Add a new record, mark the old one Superseded, and link the two records.

The supported statuses are:

  • Proposed: under discussion and not yet authoritative.
  • Accepted: the current project decision.
  • Superseded: replaced by a newer decision record.

docs.title: 0001: Separate Guidance from Runtime and Scanning
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-07-14
  • Owner: Project CodeGuard maintainers

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Project CodeGuard publishes model- and tool-agnostic security skills, rules, and reviewer guidance. Two proposals exposed important boundaries around that content:

  • Incremental scanning requires changed-file tracking, cache invalidation, and a trusted record of prior work.
  • Comprehensive secret detection requires repository-wide analysis and an evolving catalog of provider-specific patterns.

Those capabilities depend on runtime state and detection engines that CodeGuard skills and rules do not control. Embedding them in guidance would make ownership unclear and could imply detection guarantees that the project cannot provide.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• Add persistent scan state and comprehensive detection to CodeGuard. This would require runtime authority the project's guidance does not have and would duplicate dedicated scanners.
  • Implement orchestration separately for every supported host. Integrations may do this when useful, but making it the project default would fragment the model- and tool-agnostic guidance.
  • Keep CodeGuard focused on guidance while hosts own orchestration and scanners own comprehensive detection. This preserves explicit trust boundaries and avoids duplicating specialized tools.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
CodeGuard owns model- and tool-agnostic security guidance and the tooling needed to convert, validate, and package that guidance.

The consuming host or integration owns orchestration, including when guidance is invoked, which files are selected, how changes and caches are tracked, what invalidates prior results, and which state is trusted. A hook can provide an invocation point, but it does not establish state ownership or a trust boundary.

Purpose-built scanners own comprehensive detection. CodeGuard may recommend their use and provide secure guidance for findings, but it does not reproduce an exhaustive secret or vulnerability scanner.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• CodeGuard skills, rules, and reviewer bundles do not maintain incremental scan state or decide which prior results are trustworthy.
  • Host-specific integrations may implement incremental orchestration outside the model-agnostic guidance, with their trust and invalidation rules made explicit.
  • Secret-handling guidance may address coherent gaps with representative examples, while exhaustive repository, history, and provider-pattern detection remains with dedicated scanners.
  • The incremental scan proposal can close as outside CodeGuard's scope, while retaining this boundary for future proposals.

docs.title: Evaluation Results
docs.text: These pages publish results from the CodeGuard evaluation harness, which compares Semgrep findings in code written by an AI coding agent and records model usage and available cost data. Results are exploratory.

docs.title: How the evaluation works
docs.text:
• Tasks: the 121 Python tasks of the SecurityEval benchmark, each built around a known weakness.
  • Agent: the Codex coding agent, working in an isolated container with no network access. Each attempt has a turn and time limit.
  • Conditions: every model runs the same tasks three ways:
    • Baseline: the standard task prompt.
    • Secure prompt: the same prompt plus a one-sentence request to write secure code.
    • CodeGuard: the standard prompt with the CodeGuard skill installed. The agent decides whether to use it.
  • Scoring: the harness keeps the final file, checks its Python syntax, and scans it with a pinned version of Semgrep and its public rules. Generated code is never run.

docs.title: What the pages show
docs.text:
• Epochs: each pass over the cases is reported separately. For multi-epoch runs, token and cost totals use each case's final saved attempt. Retry usage recorded only for the whole run is excluded.
  • Limits: recorded turn, generation-time, case-time, and output-token caps. Shown on the report and in results.csv. Missing limits stay blank in the CSV.
  • Findings: Semgrep security findings at all confidence levels, counted on the shared cases, where every run for a model produced changed, valid code. Unchanged or invalid outputs are excluded. An attempt stopped by a limit can still contribute findings if its output passes those checks, and also counts as unfinished. Passing the checks does not establish functional correctness.
  • Likely vulnerabilities: findings from rules tagged vuln. This is a rule category, not a confidence rating.
  • High + Medium: findings from rules rated High or Medium confidence. The confidence chart shows High, Medium, and Low on the same shared cases. Low-confidence findings remain in the total.
  • Tokens per case: recorded tokens divided by all attempted cases. Includes cached input and retries. Token counts are not costs.
  • Costs: total USD and USD per case, using complete recorded costs or estimates calculated from supplied model prices. When prices are supplied, all runs use those rates. Per-case costs average all attempted cases, including unfinished ones. Every run needs a complete recorded or estimated cost.
  • Total USD vs baseline: percentage change in total USD cost from the same model's baseline, calculated from unrounded amounts. Missing costs stay blank.
  • Unfinished attempts: attempts that hit any limit or ended with an error.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Static analysis only. Findings are scanner results, not confirmed vulnerabilities, and no findings does not mean the code is secure or even correct. SecurityEval has no functional or exploit tests.
  • Limited scanner coverage. The pinned rules flag only 48 of the benchmark's 121 known-insecure reference programs, so many weaknesses go unseen.
  • One benchmark, one language. All tasks are Python.
  • Small numbers. Each epoch is one pass over 121 cases. A difference of a few findings can be chance.
  • Limits shape the results. Attempts that hit a limit leave work unfinished. Compare runs only when their settings match; each page warns when they do not.
  • Using the skill is up to the agent. Reading CodeGuard does not prove the agent followed it.

docs.title: Result sets
docs.text:
The results exporter creates the page, charts, and public CSVs together from completed harness logs.

  • CodeGuard 1.4.0 on SecurityEval
